Pele Yoetz 261:2: And regarding this the Kabbalists wrote the reason concerning the daughter of Nechunya the Well-Digger: when Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa's merit was invoked on her behalf, and he said, “Is it possible that something that righteous man was distressed over would trip up his own offspring?” she immediately rose from the pit — yet his son died of thirst (Bava Kamma 50a), because there was no one to invoke merit on his behalf. Likewise, the Holy One, blessed be He, would state halachah in the name of every sage except Rabbi Meir, since he had studied Torah from Acher [“another,” a heretic], until a certain sage came and found merit for him, saying of him, “He found a pomegranate, ate its inside, and threw away its peel,” and immediately the Holy One, blessed be He, stated halachah in his name (Chagigah 15b). And we have heard with our own ears that in a time of religious persecution, when several Jewish souls were being led out to be killed for the sanctification of the Name, a certain woman went out to meet them and said, “Master of the world, well have You known what You chose — who is like Your people, like Israel, who are killed for the sanctification of Your Name!” And a certain preacher revealed that immediately, through Deborah's words, the decree was annulled, and many such stories.
Pele Yoetz 261:3: Thus how greatly must preachers be careful, and especially during the days of judgment, the awesome days, not to arouse judgment and not to teach accusation in their sermons by mentioning the sins of the many, God forbid, but rather should say, “This is what must be done, and one must be careful of this” — let the listener listen. And if one finds himself in the synagogues of unlearned people and hears them teaching guilt against Israel and speaking wrongly, let him gird himself with strength to find merit for them even with arguments that are not clear to him, and let him say, “What can the child do and not sin — poverty has not left them a good trait, exile has not left them a good trait, and they mingled among the nations and learned their deeds, and the inclination of man's heart is evil, and they are either compelled or, for most of the people, acting unwittingly, since they do not know what the prohibition is and its severity.” This and more he should seek to judge favorably, for whoever judges others favorably, the Omnipresent judges him favorably. Go and learn how Isaac our father found merit for Israel by saying, “How many years does a man have,” etc., “dock it,” etc., “dock it,” etc. (Shabbat 89b). Examine this and understand, and you will see His kindnesses, blessed be He, for He desires kindness and accepts any kind of argument from one who seeks merit.
Pele Yoetz 261:4: And one must be especially careful, when a person is in distress, to find merit on his behalf and not to mention his sins, in the manner of frivolous people who say, “This and that caused it,” and “therefore this trouble came upon him,” for it is known that Satan accuses only at a time of danger (see Bereishit Rabbah 91:12; Shabbat 34a), and it turns out that Heaven reveals his sin and the earth rises against him. And one must be especially careful not to mention the guilt of those who dwell in the dust who are standing in judgment, and I have seen confused spirits who, when they wish to speak wrongly of those who dwell in the dust, precede by saying “Acharei Mot Kedoshim Emor” [“after the death of the holy, speak”, a wordplay on Torah portion names used as a superstitious preface], and immediately do the opposite and say “Metzora Acharei Mot” [reversing the order] — what did their remedy accomplish? And a good man speaks good of Israel and brings redemption to the world.
Pele Yoetz 261:5: And the saying of the Tanna is known (Avot 4:11): whoever commits one transgression acquires for himself one accuser, and whoever performs one commandment acquires for himself one defender. Thus this is the whole of man: that he strive with all his strength to diminish his accusers and increase his defenders through performing commandments and good deeds and Torah study, and let him not, in his poverty, hold back from adding one more defender, for this is fitting, and perhaps it will serve as a shield against calamity. And it is known that an accuser cannot become a defender; therefore he should be very careful, when performing a commandment, that it be with permissibly acquired money, and that it not be a commandment fulfilled through transgression, God forbid. And this is what the commentators explained on “in righteousness you shall be established, but on condition that you distance yourself from oppression, then you shall not fear” (Isaiah 54:14). But if he is not careful about this, our sages, of blessed memory, said of him (Yerushalmi Sukkah 3:1; Tanchuma, Emor 18), “Woe to him whose own defender becomes his accuser.”
Pele Yoetz 261:6: And since this matter is difficult, especially in these generations, who can be confident that he knows for certain which money came to him in a completely permissible way, without any hint of prohibition? Therefore the advice given is that God-fearing people should speak to one another and give each other a sum of money as a gift, making an exchange, and it should be set aside in a separate purse to do commandments and good deeds with until it is used up, and let them do this continually, for regarding money given to him as a gift he has no concern of prohibition. And one must be especially careful and diligent to do this and the like for burial shrouds, so that it not be a “garment of traitors” and their iniquities upon their bones, God forbid; and one who reflects on the matter will find it good, for it will be accepted with favor for him and he shall surely live.
Pele Yoetz 262:1: Selichot (Penitential Prayers) — The holy people of Israel rise early for Selichot from the beginning of the month of Elul. How good is their portion, that they break their desire while the nights are still short and people love to sleep, and their sleep is sweet, and the love of sleep is intense — they drive sleep from their eyes and slumber from their eyelids. Certainly by this a servant is reconciled to his Master and finds means of his own redemption, provided he does the matters properly, for otherwise he inherits a double Gehinnom — afflicting his body in this world with no benefit for the World to Come, God forbid.
Pele Yoetz 262:2: And these are the necessary conditions: let him rise promptly and wash his hands, then his face, and prepare to meet his God from head to foot as though standing before the ministers of the city, and rise early to the synagogue and say the Selichot in a hushed voice of supplication — “let the poor man speak in supplications” (Proverbs 18:23) — letter by letter, word by word, and take to heart the words he is saying and reflect deeply on them, and he will find that they are all like burning coals; and let him make his own ears hear what comes from his mouth at the beginning of the Selichot, where he says, “Let us search and examine our ways and return to You” (Lamentations 3:40), and says, “Accept in mercy those who return to You with a whole heart, their outcry.” And let a man tremble and take hold of himself, taking to heart what he has done throughout the year and throughout all his years since being in this transmigration and in other transmigrations, and what blemish he has caused in his soul and in all the worlds through the filth and impurity of the defilement of his sins, and that through our sins the Temple was destroyed and the daily offering ceased, and many other evils we have caused, and this is the pain of Heaven, and how great is our brokenness, to a degree that none of us can grasp even one part in a thousand thousand thousand. And the commentators have already explained the verse (Amos 3:4), “Will a lion roar in the forest when it has no prey?” for “aryeh” (lion) is an acronym: Elul, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Hoshana Rabbah, meaning: if a man cries out in these days, all his aim should be for the “forest” — that is, the Temple, called a forest since it has no “prey,” meaning that no sacrifices are offered due to our many sins. And let the living take to heart that on the Day of Concealment [Rosh Hashanah] he shall stand in judgment before the Judge of all the earth, an exceedingly awesome and terrible King, and the books of the living and the books of the dead are open before Him, and let him tremble with great trembling, and let the trembling of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai never leave their hearts, and let him reason a fortiori for himself on that day, all the more so, without measure.
Pele Yoetz 262:3: And the greatest reason to fear greatly and make abundant preparation is according to what the Kabbalists explained regarding the difficulty in their saying (Rosh Hashanah 16b) that there are three books: the completely righteous are inscribed and sealed at once for life, the completely wicked are inscribed and sealed at once for death, the intermediate, etc. — yet our own eyes see that the way of the wicked prospers, while the righteous man perishes and men of kindness are gathered away. And they explained that the essence of the life and death decreed on Rosh Hashanah is the life and death of the soul, and this is because a person is like one whose eyes are closed, sitting in a dark house, in darkness and the shadow of death, having two impediments: not to see the light, though it is good, and even if a lamp is brought to him, although he sees a little light, he does not benefit from the light as long as his eyes are closed — and according to the degree he opens his eyes, so he benefits from the light. So it is with this matter: man is born wild, and his eyes are closed to seeing intellectual matters, and the Holy One, blessed be He, wished to bring merit to Israel, and illuminates for them with the light of the King's countenance of life during the awesome days, illuminating the light of fear and dread.
Pele Yoetz 262:4: Thus there is no person in Israel who does not feel some fear, even one whose eyes are closed sees a little of the light, and on festivals the light of love and joy shines, and on Shabbat the light of delight, and every person feels it, all according to what the person is, and according to the preparation he makes, and according to how he strives to open his eyes — so he sees more internally: physical fear and physical love and physical delight, or the fear of exaltation and the love of exaltation and spiritual delight. And there are levels upon levels, higher and higher, and no person resembles his fellow, and according to how much he was a vessel ready to receive during these days, so illumination is drawn upon him for the rest of the days of the year to conduct himself in an order of holiness, and this is God's judgment during the awesome days regarding the life of the soul, according to one's deeds and according to one's preparation, for the wicked in their lifetimes are called dead (Berachot 18b; Tanchuma, Yitro 1). And this is the reason you see that there are people who, upon hearing words of ethics and the fear of the Lord, their uncircumcised heart is humbled and melts and becomes like water, and they entertain thoughts of repentance; while there are people whose hearts are as fat as suet, and they are heretics and deniers, and words of ethics make no impression on them, and they neither hear nor understand, for their eyes are sealed from seeing and their hearts from understanding, for they are like the dead, and the flesh of the dead does not feel the scalpel, and they go from evil to evil, Heaven have mercy. Thus, let a man be firm in strengthening himself during these days and this time, and let him do whatever is in his power to revive his soul, for the death of the soul, even for one hour, is more severe than the separation of the soul from the body, and better is one hour of repentance and good deeds than all the life of the World to Come (Avot 4:17), and therefore let him pour out his soul before the Lord that He help him for the sake of the honor of His Name, and let Israel say, “For Your Name's sake, O Lord, give us life; in Your righteousness bring our soul out of distress.”
Pele Yoetz 262:5: And even one who is unlearned and does not know what he is uttering should, in any case, say the Selichot letter by letter, word by word, with a voice of weeping, a voice of supplication, knowing the intent that he is petitioning before the King, the Lord of Hosts, for having sinned against his soul, and let him clothe himself in dread. And if he does this, let him trust in the Name of his God, for He is a gracious and merciful God, abundant in forgiveness, and does not desire the death of the dying, and does not deal tyrannically with His creatures, only that he do what is in his power to do, and “he who confesses and forsakes shall find mercy” (Proverbs 28:13).
Pele Yoetz 262:6: And the earlier authorities already cried out against reciting the Selichot hastily, for absence is better than a bad presence, and it deserves disgrace and wrath, Heaven have mercy. And the essence of these days is remembered and observed so that the living take to heart what deeds not to be done are found with him, whether in thought, speech, or deed, and take to heart to repent, and build fences and safeguards for himself so that he not return to folly again; and thereby his voice is heard when he comes to the sanctuary to say Selichot and supplications — for if he rises early for Selichot and after prayer returns to his evil ways and adds transgression to his sin, this is like one who immerses himself while holding an impure creeping thing, and God will be angry at his voice, for it is one voice paired with its own destroyer. And the commentators have already explained that this is the intent of the verse (Song of Songs 2:14), “Show me your appearance” — meaning, when you repent and wash from your filth, “then let me hear your voice,” for your voice is pleasant when your appearance is comely. Therefore the man whom the fear of the Lord has touched should, during these days, seek from books and from scholars which path light dwells in, and where he might find remedy, and do so and continue to add, so as not to relapse; and let him delve into books on the healing of the soul before the sun sets, and pursue as one pursuing life, to seek the light in the light of the King's countenance of life.
Pele Yoetz 262:7: And after Selichot, let him not fail to bear fruit, and should not follow the custom of some people who hurry through the Selichot in order to rush to be among those sitting on street corners drinking coffee and raising smoke in a gentile's shop, a session of scoffers, and to increase idle and forbidden talk there, which is forbidden all year, and certainly during these days and this time. What benefit is there to the wheat if it rises early for Selichot showing he wishes to be clean-handed and pure of heart, and afterward goes about wayward? And there are those who go back to sleep in their beds and lose the congregational prayer at its proper time, or the pains of sleep fall upon them and they doze off with their tefillin during the Shema and prayer, which is comparable to one who loses a hundred gold coins in order to earn one.
Pele Yoetz 262:8: Thus, it is good for a man to manage his affairs with judgment, doing whatever is in his power to do, and not let the addition undo the essential thing; only, if he can, let him be firm in strengthening himself to remain awake after Selichot, sitting in the synagogue or at home engaged in Torah or in supplications and requests as far as he is able, until the time of prayer, and then let him stand like a man and strengthen himself to drive sleep from his eyes and slumber from his eyelids, and pray calmly with intention of heart; and after prayer, and at every free moment, let him diminish his business and increase his engagement in Torah and the study of ethical books as far as he is able, for this is man's constant duty at all times, and all the more so during these days, when creatures are recorded to be remembered for life or for death, and great is Torah, for it gives life; and let him entertain thoughts of repentance and join a good thought to a good deed, and increase charity day by day to fulfill the verse that is written, “And break off your sin by [doing] righteousness” (Daniel 4:24), and “charity saves from death” (Proverbs 10:2), “He who pursues righteousness and kindness finds life” (ibid. 21:21). These are some points of the path for one who wishes to return to the Lord, that He have mercy on him, and to our God, for He is abundant in forgiveness. Let the wise man hear and add learning, and one who comes to purify himself is helped [from Heaven] (Shabbat 104a), in the light of the King's countenance of life, and may he be inscribed in the book of good life.
Pele Yoetz 263:1: Se'udah (Feast/Meal) — There are optional feasts and there are feasts of a commandment, and all feasts held in the company of people carry a presumption of danger, and the hour of eating is an hour of battle. Regarding optional feasts, it is itself a transgression, to the point that they said (Pesachim 49a) that a Torah scholar is not permitted to benefit from any feast that is not of a commandment, and they said that in a place where optional feasts are eaten, Satan takes the leading share among the guests and dances among them, and one transgression drags along many transgressions: excessive eating and drinking, which adds strength to the Sitra Achra, and just as a commandment performed by the many increases its strength for holiness, so correspondingly, a transgression performed by the many; and since they increase eating and drinking, filling their bellies with wicked stuff, and increase laughter, levity and mockery which accustom one to illicit relations, and many other evils, until all their tables are full of vomit and filth, Heaven have mercy.
Pele Yoetz 263:2: Therefore the God-fearing man should flee far from optional feasts as from a sword. And if sometimes he cannot say “and be clear” [i.e., avoid entirely] for the sake of peace and the like, let him accept upon himself firmly before going that he will not step out of line in eating and drinking, but rather his eating and drinking shall be measured, weighed and calibrated, and his mouth shall speak wisdom and his heart shall meditate understanding, at least between himself and himself, and let him remember the destruction of the Temple which was destroyed through our sins, and that his Master's table is empty while the delight of his own table is full of abundance, and let him grieve over this and turn the conversation to speak words of Torah and words of ethics and the fear of the Lord; and if he wishes to sing at his table, let him sing the liturgical poems that mention the Temple and the mention of sins and the like, and should not lend his hand to sing the remnants of gentile [lewd] songs, God forbid, and thereby he will merit and bring merit to others, and it is possible that the Lord will not count it as a sin for him. And let him do likewise even at a feast of a commandment, so that it not become a commandment fulfilled through transgression and so that no mishap result, and then his eating will be pleasing and counted as a commandment, and his table will be called “the table that is before the Lord.”
Pele Yoetz 264:1: Sefinah (Ship) — We have learned there (Kiddushin 82a) that sailors are mostly pious, since they see the works of the Lord and His wonders in the depths. Thus, how greatly must a person press himself and increase his expenses in order to avoid entering a ship at sea, for if all roads are presumed dangerous, how much more so seas and rivers, for it is but a hair's breadth between him and death. And if he is compelled to enter a ship according to his path, extra care is needed, and above all, to recite the Traveler's Prayer every day and to be very careful with all the commandments, and to entertain thoughts of repentance, for Satan accuses at a time of danger, and how good it is to study the Book of Psalms every day with intention and humility, for their special virtue is wondrous.
Pele Yoetz 265:1: Safek (Doubt) — Our sages, of blessed memory, already said (Avot DeRabbi Natan, ch. 30 approx.) that a doubtful transgression is harder than the transgression itself, for when a person knows he has sinned, he takes it to heart and regrets it, but regarding a doubtful transgression he issues a lenient ruling for his own soul, saying, “Perhaps I did no wrong.” It is fitting for a person to flee from transgression and to be wary of even a remote doubt even more than he flees from a sword, and our own eyes see that a sick person is concerned and guards against anything that might worsen his illness even on a remote doubt — if this is so for temporary life, how much more so for eternal life and for not angering his Creator and causing blemish and many such evils. And one who is not wary of doubt shows that he has no regard for his Maker's honor, God forbid. And I have already written on this above under the entry Chassidut — see there. And for all such cases, sitting still and not acting is preferable, and a God-fearing person fulfills his duty according to all opinions.
Pele Yoetz 266:1: Sarvanut (Refusal/Reluctance) — Too much refusal is bad, and too little is good, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 34a): one who is asked to go down before the ark [to lead prayer] should refuse the first time, begin to show some movement the second time, and the third time, stretch out his legs and go down. And they said (ibid.) that if he does not refuse at all, he is like a dish lacking salt, and if he refuses too much, he is like a dish oversalted. And likewise they said (Pesachim 66a) that one refuses for a minor but does not refuse for a great man. And the straight path is that one should not refuse and should not transgress anyone's opinion, and should nullify his own will and opinion before the will and opinion of others in matters where there is no hint of transgression, as in the saying of Rabbi Yosei, who used to say, “All my days I have never transgressed my colleagues' opinion. I know of myself that I am not a kohen, yet if my colleagues told me to go up to the platform [to bless the people], I would go up” (Shabbat 118b).
Pele Yoetz 266:2: And how much disgrace there is in the custom of the world, especially the order of refusing women [i.e., the social ritual], where the giver presses much to give and the recipient refuses much to receive, and they press one another to the point of embarrassment — this is not good. Rather, “twice, even three times, with a man” (Job 33:29): if he wishes, let him accept; and if not, let him not force it upon him against his will, but let him leave him to do as his heart desires, for a person's own will is his honor, and thereby he will get along with people and find favor and good understanding.
Pele Yoetz 267:1: Seter (Secrecy) — How great is the virtue of one who does his deeds in secret, especially regarding charity, as it is written (Proverbs 21:14), “A gift in secret subdues anger.” For one who gives charity publicly will surely be punished, as our sages, of blessed memory, said on the verse (Ecclesiastes 12:14), “For God will bring every deed into judgment, concerning every hidden thing, whether good” — this refers to one who gives charity publicly (Chagigah 5a). And they said (ibid.) that Rabbi Yannai saw a certain man giving charity publicly and said to him, “It would have been better for you not to have given it than to give it and shame him.” And many of the masses have erred in this, giving publicly, their gift small and their disgrace great; may the good Lord grant them atonement. And the early authorities have already explained the verse (Deuteronomy 16:17), “Each man according to the gift of his hand, according to the blessing of the Lord your God which He has given you” — that just as blessing rests on something hidden from the eye, so a gift to a poor person should be hidden from the eye. And the story of Mar Ukva's servant is known, who, together with his wife, entered a fiery furnace so that the poor man would not see them and be ashamed, for it is better for a person to throw himself into a fiery furnace than to shame his fellow publicly (Ketubot 67b).
Pele Yoetz 267:2: And it is true that all depends on what the person is, and on his nature, disposition and habit — there are those whose faces change color like saffron [with shame], especially if he was once wealthy and has come down and has not yet tried to receive; he needs great secrecy, for his shame is great, and one should act as I wrote under the entry Redifah [pursuit] — see there. And there are those who do not worry so much and whose hand is readily outstretched to receive, but in any case there is no person who is not embarrassed and ashamed to some degree, whether little or much, and the heart knows its own bitterness, and one must be wary of this according to its severity. Likewise, in all commandments, studies, and pious traits and the order of holiness, one who does his deeds in secret is thereby elevated and saved from the concern of arrogance and the evil eye, and it shows that his deeds are for the sake of Heaven, and wisdom is with the discreet (Proverbs 1:2), and blessing rests upon it, and the evil inclination does not rule over him, and many other such good virtues; and he should conceal his affairs even from members of his own household, unless he does it specifically for the sake of Heaven, so that they learn from him.
Pele Yoetz 268:1: Segulah (Special Remedy) — There are several things that help to restrain transgression and put an end to sin by way of a special remedy, and let the living take this to heart (Ecclesiastes 7:2) to be diligent about them, for without mortifications, fasts, or the giving of blood, his sins will be atoned for, provided he does the things properly and according to their rule, with fear and love. And if he does not take care to do so, what will he answer on the Day of Reckoning? And he will be punished doubly, whichever way you look at it, for all this is the words of our holy sages, of blessed memory, in the Talmud and Midrashim, and they are true and their words are true; and if he does not believe and mocks the words of the Sages, he is judged with boiling excrement (Eruvin 21b), and if he believes but does not fulfill them, he endangers his own soul, for he does not care to hasten his own escape with easy matters such as these, and he has no basis for exemption, and the later punishment is greater than the first, for he had no regard for his Maker's honor and his own soul. Therefore let a man be firm in strengthening himself to fulfill every one of the ways of repentance, and especially the easy matters that serve as a remedy for atonement, and let us mention these matters briefly as brought by our teacher Rabbi Yehuda Ayash, of blessed memory, in Sefer Tzipporen Shamir, and let them be a constant reminder to keep, do and fulfill, and these are they:
Pele Yoetz 268:2: Whoever answers “Amen, yehei shmei rabba” with all his strength (explanation: with all his intention and the movement of his inner limbs), even if there was a trace of heresy in him, he is forgiven (Shabbat 119b). Whoever keeps Shabbat according to its law, even if he worshipped idolatry like the generation of Enosh, he is forgiven (ibid. 118b). Whoever overlooks his own grievances, they overlook all his transgressions for him (Yoma 23a). Whoever hears an aggadic teaching from the mouth of the preacher and answers “Amen, yehei shmei rabba,” his sins are atoned for (Shocher Tov, Proverbs, ch. 10). Whoever recites the Song of the Sea with joy and pictures himself as though he himself were saved and Pharaoh and his army drowned, and recites the song, his sins are atoned for. Whoever weeps and mourns for a worthy person, all his sins are forgiven (Shabbat 105b). Whoever prays on the eve of Shabbat and says “Vayechulu,” two ministering angels say to him, “Your iniquity has departed and your sin shall be atoned for” (Shabbat 119b). Sufferings purge a person's sins, and if he accepts them with love, he will see offspring, lengthen his days, and the Lord's desire shall prosper in his hand (Berachot 5a). Whoever engages in the order of sacrifices is as though he had offered them, and all his sins are forgiven (Ta'anit 27b). Whoever engages in Torah for its own sake, his sins are atoned for (Berachot 5a), and its virtues are many, as they said in the chapter on the acquisition of Torah (Avot, ch. 6). Whoever wraps himself in tzitzit, wears tefillin, recites the Shema and prays, all his sins are forgiven (Tur, Orach Chaim, sec. 37). Whoever grieves and weeps on Yom Kippur when they read the portion Acharei Mot over the death of the righteous [Aaron's sons], the Holy One, blessed be He, proclaims over him, “Your iniquity has departed” (Zohar, Vayikra, p. 57). Whoever has a miracle performed for him and recites a song of praise, it is known that his sins are forgiven (Shocher Tov, Psalms, ch. 18).
Pele Yoetz 268:3: And how good it is to study the Book of Psalms with a voice of joyous song and thanksgiving, and one must gird himself with strength and arouse love with pure thoughts to fulfill these matters as is proper, at a time of joy, joy, and at a time of sadness, sadness, etc., provided he abandons his wicked way and does not return to folly, and does not do these things for his own honor in order that his sins be atoned for, but rather does the things for the sake of Heaven, with honor to come in the end; only let his heart understand from their special virtue that these matters are ancient and give great delight before our Father in Heaven, to the point that He pays great reward for them, and thus let his whole aim be to give delight to his Creator, and this is the whole fruit of the reward of commandments: to know, to make known, and to become known how much delight it gives. Happy is one born of woman who merits this — we have no reward greater than this, for this is the whole of man.
Pele Yoetz 269:1: Sipuk (Sufficiency/Contentment) — Contentment with the essential is a good trait, a glory to those who practice it in this world and the World to Come, and this trait is needed both in the matter of dwelling and in the matter of clothing and in the matter of eating and drinking, for we are strangers upon the earth, like a traveler who turns aside to lodge for the night on his way. What benefit is there for one to spend his strength and his days building spacious upper chambers, walls and ramparts, wash-basins and carved flower-designs, when he is destined for a burial-cave in a place narrow as a single square amah, a land of darkness and the shadow of death — would it not be better to build with that same money a trustworthy house for himself, to delight in a world where his understanding is good? And what benefit is there in wearing embroidered garments, when the hope of man is but a worm — would it not be better to prepare for his soul the covering of the cloud, the robe of the scholars? And what benefit is there in pursuing various pleasures, foods and drinks, for a moment's enjoyment as it passes through the palate, causing his soul every illness and every affliction — would it not be better to prepare delicacies for his soul for the latter days, that he delight his soul in fatness and be blessed in a world where his understanding lasts long?
Pele Yoetz 269:2: And the saying of our sages, of blessed memory, is known (Shabbat 140b): one who could eat bread of barley and eats bread of wheat transgresses “do not destroy.” And they said there that this does not apply because “do not destroy” regarding the body is more important — examine this: where “do not destroy” regarding the body does not apply [i.e., there is no health need], indeed he transgresses “do not destroy” [regarding waste of money]. And although they said (Eruvin 54a), “If you have [wealth], do good for yourself,” this means in a moderate manner according to local custom, for great is human dignity; therefore let him dress and cover himself according to what he has, according to the blessing the Lord has given him, but regarding eating and drinking, let him be sparing as much as he can on weekdays, and increase charity, and delight in eating and drinking on Shabbatot and festivals, as they explained on the saying of our sages, of blessed memory, “Let your house be open wide” — and this you can do when the poor are members of your household, that you teach yourself to feed them as the poor are fed [i.e., modestly].
Pele Yoetz 269:3: And how good would be his exchange if he reduced his expenses and sent [the savings] ahead for his soul in the World to Come, for that is his true home. And if his means are limited, let him make do with the very least and be happy with his portion, and his eye should look upon one beneath him, as Rabbi Akiva said to his wife, “See a man who does not even have straw” (Nedarim 50a). And let him give thanks for his portion and not worry at all about his lack of delighting in fine dwellings, clothing, and foods, for truly all the pleasures of this world are vanity, an illusion, and the great king who tasted and saw all pleasures already testified: in the end he said, “Vanity of vanities, said Kohelet, vanity of vanities, all is vanity” (Ecclesiastes 1:2). And who is rich? He who is happy with his portion. And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Bava Batra 110a) that of one who is not happy with his portion it is said (Proverbs 15:15), “All the days of the poor are evil,” and of one who is happy with his portion it is said (ibid.), “And a good heart has a continual feast.” And the sage said (see Mevakesh HaKedushah, Gate of Wisdom) that the order of sufficiency is half of expenditure. And how good is a word fitly spoken — there is a time to hold back and a time to spend generously, according to the place, the time, the traits of one's household, the need of the hour, and one's assets; it is good for a man to manage his affairs with judgment — a complete middle path.
Pele Yoetz 270:1: Letter Ayin: Avodat HaShem (Service of God) — Service of the blessed Name must be a complete service, a perfect service, with fear, love and great joy, in all its details, corrections and fine points, and whatever is in one's power to do, let him do, in order to fulfill a commandment properly, complete within, with intention of heart. And certainly the Holy One, blessed be He, does not deal tyrannically with His creatures (Avodah Zarah 3a), and every person is obligated only according to his own measure; and even if he serves his Creator with an incomplete service and receives his reward for his service, for the Holy One, blessed be He, does not withhold the reward of any creature — for He paid Balak the reward for the forty-two sacrifices he offered — nevertheless he will be punished for not having done as he should have done, and for not having pressed himself and entered where he could have entered, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Shabbat 31a) that on the Day of Judgment they ask him, “Why did you not engage in dialectics and in the mysteries of Torah and in the workings of the divine Chariot?”
Pele Yoetz 270:2: Now, the essence of the service of the blessed Name and the completeness of that service depend on cleaving of thought and intention of heart with fear, love, joy, and great humility, for the Merciful One desires the heart (Sanhedrin 106b) — this is a great principle in the Torah and in the service of the blessed Name. And the nearby inclination sits among the openings of the heart and turns his heart to idleness, and even at the time of our service, his heart walks in darkness with strange thoughts and evil musings, in such a way that our service is not a complete service. And the man who fears the Lord should be firm in strengthening himself to unify his heart even amid the back-and-forth [of distraction], to fear and love the honored and awesome Lord and cling to Him and serve Him with a whole heart, a complete service, a perfect service, and let him fight his inclination on this like a man of war, just as the Israelite man fights not to murder, commit adultery, or steal, for God will bring everything into judgment, and his reward for this will be great, for the reward is according to the pain. And regarding this it is said (Job 5:7), “Man is born to toil,” for great toil and labor are needed, since thought is fleeting and it is as though escaping like a fleeing bird, and one must strengthen oneself and be held in awe in holiness, and remove the stumbling stone from his heart — otherwise, only thoughts of holiness should be considered, not evil musings.
Pele Yoetz 271:1: Anavah (Humility) — Humility is a good trait unlike any other, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Avodah Zarah 20b), humility is greater than all of them; it is the father of the Torah and of good traits, and its companions follow after it: love and brotherhood, peace and friendship with every person, and one who has it does not become angry at all, overlooks his own grievances, his spirit is a broken spirit, his heart is a broken and contrite heart, he is not particular about anything, flees from honor, does not seek greatness, does not covet honor, and does not take credit for himself, and many other good and upright traits truly follow from humility; and according to its praise and goodness, it is hard to find, and a person must overcome his inclination like a man with constant pure thoughts, always considering: what is man, a mere breath? And he should wage war with strategies against his inclination, which entices him to let his heart be lifted up and become an abomination to the Lord, and let it not depart from his mouth and his thought to say, “What are we and what is our life, what is our strength and what is our righteousness — are not all the mighty as nothing, and men of renown as though they had never been, and the wise as lacking knowledge, and the understanding as lacking sense, for all our deeds are chaos and the days of our lives are vanity?”
Pele Yoetz 271:2: And even if he has attained mighty Torah and commandments like Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, what good is it to him if his heart is lifted up, since it is an abomination to the Lord, and he is then like one of the worthless and base — why should he have life, since the Holy One, blessed be He, says of him that He and he cannot dwell together (see Sotah 5a; Arachin 15b), and “the high He knows from afar,” and his dust will not be stirred at the resurrection of the dead, and many such evils. Therefore let a man be firm in strengthening himself with great vigor to humble himself, and let him consider that according to the abundance of his wisdom, understanding, and ability, his obligation to serve is greater, and the Holy One, blessed be He, is exacting with him to a hairsbreadth. To what is the matter comparable? To two who owed the king money — one owed a thousand gold dinars, and one owed a thousand silver [dinars]. The one who owed a thousand silver paid five hundred, and the other paid five hundred gold dinars. It turns out that the one who paid five hundred gold dinars remains owing much more than the one who gave only five hundred of silver. So it is with this matter.
Pele Yoetz 271:3: And a person is obligated to say, “With what shall I approach the Lord? Let me bow before the God on high” (Micah 6:6), for He has increased His goodness toward me and graced me with a little understanding, and helped me to do a little more good than others — this is a good greater than all the life of this world and all the life of the World to Come; “I am unworthy of all the kindnesses and all the truth” (Genesis 32:11), and with whatever I do I cannot fulfill my duty for this good alone. And this was the reasoning of Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, who was more humble than any man. And let him also constantly hold his own sin before him and say, “Why should I take pride in the honor given to me, since people do not know me? Do I not know my own transgression, and my sins, which if my neighbors were to smell them, they would distance themselves from me and from my territory? This too is among the goodnesses of the Creator toward me, that my sin is covered.” And in this orphaned generation, it is easy for a person of understanding to grasp his own lowliness, his limited worth, his short grasp, and his great deficiency in serving his Creator, that he has not done even one part in a thousand thousand thousand of what is incumbent on him, and the sins of his youth, and new and old, layer upon layer. Thus let him always do this, and let the living take to heart this and the like, matters that humble the heart.
Pele Yoetz 271:4: And one must be especially careful when preaching before the public and when being honored and the like, for the nearby inclination entices with a double enticement so that his heart enjoy it and he seek greatness and covet honor — let him immediately gird himself with strength and hasten to find escape for himself with pure thoughts, and let him also say pure words with his mouth, as Rav said when he saw a crowd of Sages following him: “If his loftiness ascends to the heavens... he shall perish forever like his own dung” (Yoma 87a). And let his heart cry out to his Father that He help him for the sake of the honor of His Name and save him from descending to the pit — then his heart will be humbled and he will be despised and loathsome in his own eyes, and the Lord will not withhold good.
Pele Yoetz 272:1: Ashirut (Wealth) — Wealth is a stronger trial than poverty, for it is prone to lead to several prohibitions and many evils, and requires extra care and great vigilance not to let his heart be lifted up above his brethren, and not to answer boldly, and not to crush the poor at the gate, and not to stop up his ear from the cry of the poor, but rather to surely hear his cry and open his hand wide to him and surely give to him, and grant him sufficient for whatever he lacks (Deuteronomy 15:8, 14). And his hand should be open to support those who study Torah and to strengthen faltering knees and to be a support to the fallen with gracious and kind loans, and to increase in commandments and good deeds according to the blessing the Lord has given him. And let him always tremble and take hold of himself at the story of the daughter of Nakdimon ben Gurion, as brought in the Talmud (Ketubot 66b), and have regard for himself lest he too has not done what he should have done. And how good it would be if he brought the tithe to the house of the Lord, for then his heart would be settled that he had fulfilled his duty, and he should not spend his wealth excessively on vanity and emptiness, but rather let his money be used to do his Creator's will and to acquire life in the World to Come through it. And let him increase giving gifts in secret so that the recipient not be shamed. And let him not seek greatness and not covet honor, and not take credit for himself for distributing his charity, for he is only like a trustee for the poor, giving them what is theirs, performing an errand of his Master, yet it shall be counted to him as righteousness, and he shall receive good reward, in such a way that the poor man does more for him than the rich man does for the poor man, meriting abundant good, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Ruth Rabbah 5:9) on the verse, “The man with whom I worked today is named Boaz” [implying Boaz gained more]. And let him gladden the heart of the downtrodden with his good words. And the saying of our sages, of blessed memory, is known (Bava Batra 9b) that one who gives charity is blessed with six blessings, and one who appeases the poor man with words is blessed with eleven blessings. And let him honor them, lift them up, and exalt them for the honor of the blessed Name, for he stands at the right hand of the needy, and let them be invited guests in his house at the height of his joy, and let his house be open wide (Avot 1:4), and let the poor be members of his household (ibid. 1:5), and let his house be a meeting place for the wise (ibid. 1:4), and let him take to heart that this is his portion from all his labor, that he send before him the light of a commandment and the light of Torah, which he shall eat by, and delight his soul in fatness.
Pele Yoetz 272:2: And let him diminish his business and engage in Torah. If he knows how to read, let him read, and if not, let him go to a sage and have him teach him, and in any case, even if his business is abundant and he is busy with his affairs, he should not fail to pray morning, afternoon, and evening with the congregation and to fix times for Torah, and he should study ethical books or hear teachings from books and from scholars about which path light dwells in, so that he not be one who neglects the Torah due to abundant wealth, which in the end causes him to neglect it due to poverty (Avot 4:9). And it is known that wealth and abundant business do not exempt the wealthy man from serving his Creator, and this is not a way to remove him from transgression, for they said (Yoma 35b) that Hillel condemns the poor and Rabbi Elazar ben Charsom condemns the wealthy on the Day of Judgment. And even if he supports those who study Torah, giving him grounds for exemption for not engaging in Torah all day, coming to his reward like Yissachar and Zevulun, nevertheless this does not exempt him from praying with the congregation and from fixing times for Torah and from engaging in Torah at every free moment, in order to learn to fear the Lord and to do what is incumbent upon him to do; and if a man were to give all the wealth of his house in order to be exempt from the commandments and do as his heart desires, he would be utterly scorned (Song of Songs 8:7).
Pele Yoetz 272:3: And let not the rich man boast of his riches except in doing kindness, justice and righteousness (Jeremiah 9:22-23), and let his heart not be lifted up, for his body is not his money, and in the abundance of good, let him remember the days of adversity destined to come upon him, and let the day of death be before his eyes, for there rich and poor meet and are equal. And they said that the initial letters of “ashir” [rich] mean “let the rich man humble himself, for his hope is high [i.e., precarious].” And whatever is in his power to do good with his body and his money, let him do, and let his eye not be sated from distributing his money. Also let him do good for himself and his own flesh, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Eruvin 54a), “My son, if you have, do good for yourself,” and let him clothe himself with what he has and honor his wife and somewhat increase the honor of his house, and make himself a dwelling befitting his honor, a middle path, in such a manner that he has settlement for serving his Creator and receiving guests.
Pele Yoetz 272:4: Likewise let him spend his money to reduce business and trouble, and let him have servants who serve him within and without, so that he be free, on the one hand, to engage in Torah and to serve his Creator. Likewise let him spend his money and not be stingy, so as not to travel on roads and not enter into dangers, and not rely on a miracle, but rather live a life of ease like a king among his troops, for what advantage has a man in his toil that he toils, and what benefit is it that the Lord has graced him with wealth and possessions if he lives a life of hardship and does not toil in Torah? Therefore let him choose to rejoice in his portion and enjoy his wealth according to the blessing the Lord has given him, and “a man's gift makes room for him” (Proverbs 18:16) in this world and the World to Come, and let his wealth be kept by its owner for his own benefit, for his body and his soul.
Pele Yoetz 273:1: Onah (Conjugal Duty) — Onah is one of the six hundred thirteen commandments, as it is written (Exodus 21:10), “And her conjugal rights he shall not diminish.” And of such a matter it is said (Hosea 14:10), “For the ways of the Lord are right, and the righteous walk in them, but transgressors stumble in them.” And it all follows the intention of the heart: if he intends it for the sake of a commandment, this is a commandment, and he receives reward for it like one who lays tefillin and like other Torah commandments; but if he intends it for his own pleasure, to satisfy his inclination, he becomes base within the license of the Torah, and regarding this the Torah commanded (Leviticus 19:2), “You shall be holy” — be separated, sanctify yourself in what is permitted to you. And the manner of performing this commandment for the sake of a commandment is that he give its fruit in its proper time according to his obligation at the time stated in the Torah, and that it be after midnight, all according to what the person is, as I wrote above under the entry Zivug [Union].
Pele Yoetz 273:2: And let his intention be for the sake of a commandment, for the sake of the unification of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, to repair matters at their root in the supernal realm. And if he intends it to fulfill the commandment of procreation and to bring forth many offspring who serve the Lord, is this not good? (And if his wife longs for him and desires reconciliation with him, it is a great commandment to fulfill her needs, and this is the essence of the commandment of onah according to the mystical meaning of the matter, and she will have understanding children, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Nedarim 20b).) And if he intends it in order to be satisfied and not come to prohibition, this too is good, except that our sages, of blessed memory, already said (Sukkah 52b) that it satisfies him with hunger and starves him with satiety [i.e., indulgence increases desire rather than satisfying it]. Therefore let him manage his affairs with judgment, according to what he is, according to his strength and his nature, and let all his deeds be for the sake of Heaven (and the remaining warnings and the order fitting to sanctify oneself at the time of intimacy are already written above under the entry Zivug).
Pele Yoetz 274:1: Iyun (Careful Study/Deliberation) — Careful study is exceedingly necessary for everything. Regarding the wisdom of Torah, they already said (Berachot 6b) that the reward of a teaching is [determined by] its reasoning, for one should apply his mind to examine the depth of the halachah and to engage in dialectics with difficulties and resolutions, in order to separate chaff and straw from the grain, and to purify the halachah, whitening it from the grip of the husks, and to adorn the bride — the letters of “halachah.” Likewise regarding legal judgment, one must engage in careful study to bring forth a true judgment of truth. Likewise for all mundane matters, great care and study is needed for every deed and every word, whether to do it or refrain, and how and in what manner it is proper to do it, and one who reflects on the matter will find good. And this is a great principle: a person should not be wise in his own eyes and should not rely on his own understanding at first glance, for Scripture says (Psalms 116:11), “I said in my haste, all men are liars.”
